Sprayberry STEM Moon Explorers 1 
 
Faven Yacob, Nathan McGar, Harlow Zellers, Omotese Aikhuele, Garrett Lynch 
Team #23441  
High School Division    
Sprayberry STEM Academy

Background 
Scientists need to develop independent life support systems for lunar missions to achieve 
successful long-term exploration because these systems will reduce the requirement for costly 
Earth-based supply deliveries. The lunar agricultural system provides astronauts with fresh food 
through sustainable practices which supports their physical health through nutritious food and 
their mental health during extended space missions (NASA, 2019). The development of 
dependable plant cultivation systems for Moon surfaces will create essential nutrients which 
enables humans to maintain health while in space. 
Lunar regolith differs significantly from Earth soil in both structure and composition. It 
lacks organic matter and contains minimal bioavailable nutrients, conditions that often result in 
stunted plant growth or complete failure when conventional crops are grown directly within it. 
The regolith surface creates difficulties for plant growth because its rocky composition blocks 
root penetration which prevents water absorption. The current conditions of lunar regolith make 
direct cultivation of plants in this soil type unsuccessful until scientists develop suitable 
modifications. For this reason, selecting crops that are naturally adapted to harsh, nutrient-poor 
environments is essential for lunar agricultural research. 
 
In this experiment, we use Vigna unguiculata, commonly known as cowpeas as our crop. 
The specific root structure of cowpeas together with their ability to thrive in different 
environments makes them an ideal crop for lunar farming operations. The plants thrive best in 
dry environments which include hot desert areas with drought conditions and weak soil and 
insufficient water supply and low phosphorus levels (Sheahan, 2012). The plant survives harsh 
environmental conditions because it developed a strong taproot which enables it to find water in

the soil while staying stable in areas with poor nutrients and rocky surfaces (Poudel et al.,2025). 
The characteristics of cowpeas match the difficulties which lunar regolith presents so they show 
potential for lunar soil cultivation. 
 
The process of plant development depends on two essential factors which include soil 
composition and gravitational forces. On Earth, plants rely on gravitropism, the ability of roots to 
sense and grow in the direction of gravitational pull (Herranz & Medina, 2014). Plants lose their 
ability to detect gravity when they experience microgravity or reduced-gravity conditions which 
occur during Moon missions where gravity operates at one-sixth of Earth's strength. Plants that 
lose their root orientation will grow randomly which leads to poor space utilization and poor soil 
attachment and reduced water and nutrient access(Kiss, 2015). Research done demonstrates that 
plant roots become smaller while the complete plant mass reduces, which would result in major 
crop production reductions unless suitable solutions are developed (Ferl & Paul, 2016). The use 
of water resources becomes less efficient when root systems lose their ability to absorb water 
effectively which results in decreased food production for lunar space exploration. 
 
The natural geotropic behavior of cowpeas leads their taproots to grow downward 
because they follow Earth's gravitational force. In the absence of a dominant gravitational cue, 
such as on the Moon, this natural growth behavior becomes unreliable. Roots will develop 
randomly when there is no correct direction to follow which will decrease the productivity of 
restricted farming areas. The success of lunar crop cultivation depends on establishing an 
alternative cue which can function as a substitute for gravity. 
 
Hydrogels show promise as a solution to this issue. Hydrogels function as water-
absorbing polymers which possess the ability to hold substantial water content while releasing

water at controlled rates during extended periods. In our team’s previous experiment, Evaluating 
the Comparative Advantages of Hydrogels Versus Traditional Wicking Watering Method Across 
Uniform Layers of Earth and Lunar Regolith on the Growth of Vigna unguiculata (Brathwaite et 
al.,2024), hydrogels significantly improved plant growth in lunar regolith simulant by delivering 
water precisely where it was needed. The specific water delivery system achieved two main 
benefits which included waste reduction and enhanced resource management efficiency for 
space-based agricultural operations. 
 
Our study explores a novel application of hydrogels, controlling root directionality. The 
placement of hydrogels throughout the growth medium serves to establish artificial directional 
signals which root growth will follow. Roots will tend to move toward regions with better water 
access when there are no powerful gravitational forces present. The application of hydrogels 
through this method enables root organization into structured patterns which help roots adapt to 
lower gravitational forces. The ability to direct root growth would allow farmers to optimize 
space usage and increase planting numbers which would lead to enhanced crop yields within the 
limited lunar habitat space. The method would serve as a vital component to establish sustainable 
lunar farming operations which would enable humans to stay on the Moon permanently. 
Hypothesis 
Our team predicted that Vigna unguiculata roots will grow toward the hydrogel source. 
This experiment tests how hydrotropism influences root directionality and determines if hydrogel 
placement is a reliable predictor of root growth patterns in lunar regolith.

Experimental Design 
 
Based on the success of one of our previous experiments (Brathwaite et al., 2024), our team 
adopted an ant farm design. The design was successful for its visibility advantages due to the 
windows on each side of the farm, making data collection and root health monitoring efficient. The 
current design also implements the irrigation system that was refined through previous experiments 
to distribute water in a controllable way and remain accessible to the plant. The use of this irrigation 
system is to negate the threat water poses to plants in microgravity, as water would otherwise cling 
to the plant and deprive it of oxygen.

Each farm has a standardized watering system that utilizes hydrogel’s unique ability to 
capture/retain water as a means of a water source. This watering system connects through a back 
panel of the farm to supply equal amounts of water to the differently arranged hydrogel sources 
(Figure 1). 
Each container is made up of two 20.32 x 25.4 cm glass panes set 1.27 cm apart from each 
other and is held together by 3D printed structures made of PLA plastic, shown in Figures 2 and 3. 
Each container holds exactly one seed, this was done in response to the change in regolith volume 
new to this years competition. A central part of the experiment was to test the effects of vertical 
hydrogel sources placed at different distances from the seed. Each trial included a wide growing 
section and a narrow vertical hydrogel water source section, with the hydrogel placed at increasing 
distances from the side frame: 1 inch for Trial 1, 2 inches for Trial 2. In this way, each trial’s roots 
were able to demonstrate hydrotropism at different intensities depending on its initial distance from

the water source. As a control, there was also a third trial with a horizontal hydrogel source, in 
which the water was accessible evenly for our plant’s roots and could follow natural growth trends. 
Though our growth period was five weeks long, our team decided to meet up 3 times per 
week to collect data. Each time our team met up to collect data, three designated team members 
would grab their assigned trial/farm to begin data collection for the day. Each trial was measured by 
recording data points such as: plant height from the top of the soil in centimeters, root distance from 
the point in which the seed was planted in centimeters, and the amount of water remaining in the 
source beaker in milliliters to a spreadsheet for further analysis. At the end of the measuring process 
the beaker/water source was refilled up to 250 milliliters, no matter the water volume before 
measuring. 
Variables 
The independent variable in this experiment was the distance of the hydrogel from the 
plant frame. Our team conducted three trials to determine which root direction would occur when 
hydrogel was used for placement. In Trial 1, the hydrogel was positioned 1 inch from the frame. 
In Trial 2, the hydrogel was placed 2 inches from the frame. The control trial of Trial 3 used a 
horizontal hydrogel layer which was placed 1 inch above the growth farm. Data was collected to 
determine which hydrogel distance produced the most significant change in root growth and 
directionality in the crops. 
 
The dependent variable was the rate and direction of root growth toward the hydrogel 
across the three trials. Our team used qualitative and quantitative data collection methods to 
study plant root development at different time intervals. Our team collected measurements and 
observations throughout Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Fridays and documented plant development

through photographic records on these specific days. This allowed for comparison of which 
hydrogel distance had the greatest effect on plant growth under these conditions. 
All plants were grown under a single fume hood covered with UV film to block external 
UV rays. The experiment used one plant per farm for each trial while keeping the water amount 
in beakers at 250ml with distilled water. A single growth light was provided for each trial and 
remained on throughout the school day. Vigna unguiculata was the plant species in all trials and 
was grown in a 25% Earth soil and 75% lunar regolith soil composition. 
Results 
 
 
 
 
 
The most important trend appeared in the root growth toward the hydrogel data. The root 
system in Trial 1 continued to grow without pause from October 22 until November 7 before it

became dormant until November 21 when the hydrogel reached 1 inch from the frame. The roots 
followed the water source because the hydrogel placement near the plant resulted in successful 
root direction. 
 
The root growth in Trial 2 showed an initial increase when the hydrogel was positioned 2 
inches from the frame during the period from October 22 to October 25 but it subsequently 
decreased until November 1 before showing some recovery during November 14. The changing 
pattern of root growth indicates that increased hydrogel separation between the roots made the 
directional moisture signal less effective which resulted in reduced root direction accuracy. The 
control trial demonstrated root growth persistence until November 7 but the roots extended 
directly into the ground without any orientation toward water sources thus lacking directional 
growth control. 
The experiments showed that root development expanded from October 22 until 
November 7 before it reached a stable point which continued until November 21. The growth 
frames reached their maximum capacity at the same point in every trial which indicates their 
physical constraints rather than plant health deterioration caused this stabilization. The plants 
maintained their aboveground growth throughout the research period while their plants stayed in 
good health although their seed germination took longer than anticipated. 
 The research data indicates that hydrogel placement affects root growth patterns because the 
hydrogel provides the most effective root direction when it is positioned 1 inch away from the 
frame.

pages.text:
Conclusion 
Our results indicate that hydrogel placement at specific locations can establish artificial 
growth directions through moisture distribution, which leads roots toward specific directions 
when gravitational forces are weak. The experimental data obtained will help researchers design 
upcoming investigations to determine how hydrogel amount and position and water amount 
affect root growth. The study needs improvement through two main aspects which involve 
decreasing water intake and minimizing the amount of hydrogel used. The experiment would 
produce better evidence about hydrogel guidance, causing directionality if maintaining a fixed 
200 mL water volume at the start. Using a reduced and controlled water amount would also help 
determine whether directionality can be achieved with less water, making the system more cost-
efficient and practical for future applications. The results establish essential knowledge which 
will help scientists develop better hydrogel-based systems for space-efficient lunar crop 
cultivation. 
 
Week 5(11/17-11/21) 
• Half of the root system established direct contact 
with hydrogel. 
• Roots on the side closest to the hydrogel were 
noticeably longer and more developed, while roots 
on the opposite side, away from the hydrogel, 
remained smaller.
